'''The Cheviot''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|tʃ|iː|v|i|ə|t}}) is an [[extinct volcano]] and the highest [[Summit (topography)|summit]] in the [[Cheviot Hills]] and in the county of [[Northumberland]].<ref name=Bathurst_2012/><ref name="hall">{{cite book |last1=Hall |first1=Gemma |title=Slow Northumberland and Durham |date=2012 |publisher=Bradt Travel Guides |location=Slow Northumberland and Durham - Including Newcastle, Hadrian's Wall and the Coast |isbn=9781841624334}}</ref> Located in the extreme north of [[England]], it is a {{convert|1+1/4|mi|km|abbr=off|0|adj=on}} walk from the [[Scotland|Scottish]] border and, with a height of {{convert|2,674|ft|m|abbr=off|0}} above sea-level, is located on the northernmost few miles of the [[Pennine Way]],<ref name="NTBNP" /> before the descent into [[Kirk Yetholm]].

The Cheviot was formed when melting in the crust over 390 million years ago gave rise to volcanic activity, producing a [[stratovolcano]] and [[Igneous intrusion|pluton]], and it has subsequently sustained intense erosion.<ref name="GHN" /> Several watercourses radiate from The Cheviot.<ref name="CLTranquil">[https://www.chroniclelive.co.uk/news/north-east-news/how-tranquil-part-north-east-16324228] How this tranquil part of the North East is far from the madding crowd
. Chronicle Live. Retrieved November 28, 2021.</ref>

==Etymology==
The name ''Cheviot'', which was first documented in 1181 as ''Chiuiet'',<ref name="pnnd">{{cite book |last1=Mawer |first1=Allen |title=The Place-Names of Northumberland and Durham |date=1920 |publisher=University Press |page=44 |url=https://archive.org/stream/cu31924028042996/cu31924028042996_djvu.txt |access-date=22 March 2021}}</ref> is probably of [[Common Brittonic|Brittonic]] origin.<ref name="bliton">{{cite web |last1=James |first1=Alan |title=A Guide to the Place-Name Evidence |url=http://spns.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Alan_James_Brittonic_Language_in_the_Old_North_BLITON_Volume_II_Dictionary.pdf |website=SPNS - The Brittonic Language in the Old North |access-date=25 November 2018 |archive-date=13 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170813011121/http://spns.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Alan_James_Brittonic_Language_in_the_Old_North_BLITON_Volume_II_Dictionary.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The name involves the element ''*ceμ-'', meaning "a ridge", and the nominal suffix ''-ed'', which in place-names can mean "having the quality of" (cf. [[Chevet, West Yorkshire|Chevet]], Yorks.). The final syllable may have been influenced by [[Old English]] ''geat'' ("a gate")<ref name="bliton" /> The inclusion of the definite article in its name is optional, with some hillwalkers simply referring to the mountain as 'Cheviot'.

== Geography ==
At {{convert|2,674|ft|m|abbr=off|0}} above sea-level, The Cheviot is the highest point in the [[Cheviot Hills]], the [[county top]] of [[Northumberland]], England's highest point outside of Cumbria and fourth-highest outside the Lake District, after Cross Fell, Great Dun Fell and Little Dun Fell.<ref name="Jones2012">{{cite book |last1=Jones |first1=Paul Anthony |title=The British Isles - A Traveler Gazetteer |date=7 November 2012 |publisher=Summerdale Publishers LTD |isbn=9780857658159 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A0j0CQAAQBAJ |access-date=22 September 2022}}</ref><ref name="bordersbanks">{{cite book |last1=Banks |first1=Francis Richard |title=The Borders |date=1977 |publisher=Batsford |isbn=9780713402896 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2CIjAAAAMAAJ |access-date=22 September 2022}}</ref> Assuming that summits on the border are classed as both Scottish and English, if prominence criteria are disregarded, its subsidiary summit, Cairn Hill West Top, or Hangingstone Hill, is the most easterly mountain in Scotland.

It is located in the [[Northumberland National Park]] and is {{convert|41|mi|km|abbr=off|0}} from the city of [[Newcastle-upon-Tyne]].<ref name="chpan" /> It can be viewed in the distance from the peak of Cow Hill on the [[Town Moor, Newcastle upon Tyne|Town Moor]], the city's largest park.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://kaleelzibe.com/bbc-town-moor-project/ | title=BBC Town Moor project | date=19 February 2015 }}</ref> The mountain can also be viewed from most areas of Northumberland and from as far south as central County Durham. The Cheviot's summit boasts views of many upland areas such as the [[Lake District]], including [[Scafell Pike]] (England's highest mountain) over 80 miles to the south-west, the North Pennines and the [[North York Moors]] in Northern England, as well as several in Scotland including the [[Ettrick Hills]], the [[Pentland Hills|Pentlands]] and even the southern peaks of the [[Grampian Mountains|Grampians]] and the [[Mounth]].<ref name="chpan" /> The summit is a triangular [[plateau]] covered with [[peat]] quagmires.<ref name="ntb9257">{{cite book |last1=Pevsner |first1=Nikolaus |last2=Richmond |first2=Ian Archibald |last3=Grundy |first3=John |last4=Ryder |first4=Peter |last5=McCombie |first5=Grace |last6=Welfare |first6=Humphrey |title=Northumberland |date=11 March 1992 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=9780300096385}}</ref>

[[File:Hen Hole - geograph.org.uk - 48620.jpg|left|thumb|Hen Hole, a gorge that marks the start of the College valley on the Cheviot.]]
[[Usway Burn]], a tributary of the [[River Coquet|Coquet]], rises on The Cheviot, as does College Burn, which flows across a series of [[waterfall|cascades]] though a [[Canyon|gorge]] known as [[Hen Hole]] on the western flank of the mountain and merges with the [[Bowmont Water]] to form the [[River Glen, Northumberland|River Glen]] near Kirk Newton. Harthope Burn also has its source at the Cheviot.<ref name="nsm1835">{{cite book |title=New Sporting Magazine - Volume 9 |date=1835 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5oUEAAAAQAAJ}}</ref><ref name="ntb1913">{{cite book |last1=Haselhurst |first1=S Rennie |title=Northumberland |date=1913 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781107677500 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FLRvFIqbhFgC |access-date=10 June 2021}}</ref><ref name="NTBNP">{{cite web |url=https://www.northumberlandnationalpark.org.uk/ |title= The Cheviot |website=Northumberland National Park |access-date=27 November 2021}}</ref><ref name="fnorth">{{cite news |title=Hen Hole in Wooler |url=https://fabulousnorth.com/hen-hole/ |access-date=21 March 2024 |work=Fabulous North}}</ref>

== Geology ==
[[File:Mt_Etna_and_Catania1.jpg|right|thumb|During the geological era in which it was active, The Cheviot volcano may have been similar in size to [[Mount Etna]] on Sicily (pictured).<ref name="ntbnpvol">{{cite web |title=Walking in a volcano. |url=https://www.northumberlandnationalpark.org.uk/events/walking-in-a-volcano/event-3669/ |access-date=10 June 2021}}</ref>]]
The Cheviot is an extinct [[stratovolcano]] eruptive during the [[Caledonian orogeny]] (490–390 Ma), in which volcanic activity arose from melting within the [[earth's crust|mantle crust]].<ref name="flodden">{{cite web |last1=Kille |first1=Ian |title=15. Geology of the battlefield and wider landscape |url=https://www.flodden1513ecomuseum.org/project/flodden-an-ancient-landscape/15-geology-of-the-battlefield-and-wider-landscape |website=Flodden 1513 |access-date=19 November 2020}}</ref><ref name="GHN">Geological history of Northumbria. Yorkshire Geological Society. Retrieved November 28, 2021.</ref> The mountain is heavily eroded, and originally may have been as high as {{convert|10,000|ft|m|abbr=on}}, with a diameter perhaps of {{convert|37|mi|km}}.<ref name="flodden" /><ref name="vms">{{cite book |last1=Upton |first1=B. G. J. |title=Volcanoes and the Making of Scotland |date=2015 |publisher=Dunedin Academic Press Ltd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fVxwDwAAQBAJ |isbn=978-1780465418 |access-date=14 August 2019}}</ref> [[Volcanic vents]] may have been located along the faults at Harthope and Thirl Moor.<ref name="GeoNorth" /> The earliest volcanic activity in the area was violent and explosive, with exposed ash and [[ignimbrite]] showing [[pyroclastic flow]]s to have reached [[Coquetdale]] and [[Ingram, Northumberland|Ingram]].<ref name="GeoNorth">{{cite web |title=The Cheviot Hills |url=https://www.geologynorth.uk/the-cheviot-hills/ |website=Geology North |access-date=22 March 2021 |archive-date=26 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191226111501/http://www.geologynorth.uk/the-cheviot-hills/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Later activity consisted of [[andesitic]], [[trachyte]] and [[rhyolitic]] lava extrusion, which abnormally for such lavas, covered an area as large as {{convert|600|km2|sqmi|order=flip|abbr=on}}.<ref name="GeoNorth" /> Lavas erupted from the Cheviot form the rocks that underlie [[Branxton, Northumberland|Branxton]] and [[Flodden|Flodden Ridge]].<ref name="flodden" />

[[Granitic]] magma was intruded into the layers of lava during the time period immediately before the volcano became inactive. The resulting {{convert|50|km2|sqmi|order=flip|abbr=on}} [[pluton]] was exposed by erosion during the [[Carboniferous]] (+298 Ma).<ref name="GeoNorth" />

[[Glacial till]] is common in the area, which is a remnant of the [[Last Glacial Period|Last Ice Age]] (< 115 Ka), during which the Cheviots were beneath ice sheets.<ref name="earthw1" /> The peat expanses date from the immediately post-glacial period.<ref name="earthw1" />

== Human history ==
Flattened remnants of a [[Neolithic]] [[henge monument]] have been uncovered at nearby [[Hethpool]].<ref name="collegevaley" />  The stone circle may date to around 2500 BC, and is hypothesized to have been a ritualistic gateway to the mountain.<ref name="collegevaley" />

Harthope Burn, which cuts a deep valley on the flanks of The Cheviot, marked the boundary between the [[Border reivers|reivers]] of the English East and [[Scottish Marches|Middle Marches]] in the 16th and 17th century.<ref name="keytopast">{{cite journal |title=Earle (Northumberland) |url=http://www.keystothepast.info/article/10339/Site-Details?PRN=N13768 |website=Key to the Past|date = 4 November 2016}}</ref>

[[Image:B17 Undercarriage The Cheviot.jpg|thumb|The landing gear of a [[B-17]] bomber that crashed in [[World War II]]]]
During [[World War II]], The Cheviot and the hills surrounding it were the site of aircraft crashes which claimed the lives both of [[Allied forces (World War II)|Allied]] and German airmen.<ref name="collegevaley">{{cite web |title=Historical Sites |url=https://www.college-valley.co.uk/about-us/historical-sites/ |website=College Valley |access-date=22 March 2021}}</ref> A local shepherd John Dagg and his sheepdog rescued a pilot following an [[Royal Air Force|RAF]] crash in 1942.<ref name="chronicle14" /> Dagg also rescued survivors of a crash in December 1944, which killed 2 members of a 9-man [[US Air Force]] crew.<ref name="chronicle14">{{cite news |last1=Daniel |first1=Brian |title=Aircrew remembered at ceremony 70 years on from crash in the Northumberland Cheviot Hills |url=https://www.chroniclelive.co.uk/news/north-east-news/aircrew-remembered-ceremony-70-years-8318086 |access-date=22 March 2021 |date=19 December 2014}}</ref> Aircraft wreckage is still seen on the mountain today.

== Access ==
Other than the route via the Pennine Way, most routes up the Cheviot start from the Harthope Burn side to the northeast, which provides the nearest access by road. The summit is around {{convert|3|mi|km|0|abbr=on}} from the road-end at Langleeford; across the valley to the east is the rounded peak of [[Hedgehope Hill|Hedgehope]]. There are routes following the ridges above either side of the valley, and a route that sticks to the valley floor until it climbs to the summit of the Cheviot from the [[head of the valley]].

Although the Pennine Way does a {{convert|2|mi|km|0|abbr=on}} out-and-back detour to the Cheviot, many walkers who come this way omit it, since the stage (the most northerly) is {{convert|29|mi|km|0|abbr=on}} long.

[[Image:The Cheviot Summit.jpg|thumb|The [[Pennine Way]] approaching the summit of The Cheviot on the flag stone path]]
[[Image:Harthope Valley - Cheviots - geograph.org.uk - 326148.jpg|thumb|The Cheviot and the Harthope Valley]]

==View==
The view is obscured greatly by the flatness of the summit plateau. Nevertheless, on a clear day the following are visible (from west, clockwise); [[Broad Law]], [[Moorfoot Hills]], [[Pentland Hills]], the [[Ochils]], [[Lammermuir Hills]], [[Ros Hill]], [[Long Crag]], [[Urra Moor]], [[Tosson Hill]], [[Burnhope Seat]], [[Cross Fell]], [[Helvellyn]], [[Scafell Pike]], [[Skiddaw]], [[Sighty Crag]], [[Peel Fell]], and [[Queensberry (hill)|Queensberry]]. The longest possible line of sight from the Cheviot is to [[Beinn a' Ghlò]], {{convert|112|mi|km|0|abbr=off}} away in the [[Grampians]] of the [[Scottish Highlands]].<ref name="chpan">{{cite web |title=Cheviot - Panoramas |url=https://www.viewfinderpanoramas.org/panoramas/ENG/CHEVIOT.gif |access-date=27 September 2024}}</ref>

extract:
The Cheviot () is an extinct volcano and the highest summit in the Cheviot Hills and in the county of Northumberland. Located in the extreme north of England, it is a 1+1⁄4-mile (2-kilometre) walk from the Scottish border and, with a height of 2,674 feet (815 metres) above sea-level, is located on the northernmost few miles of the Pennine Way, before the descent into Kirk Yetholm.
The Cheviot was formed when melting in the crust over 390 million years ago gave rise to volcanic activity, producing a stratovolcano and pluton, and it has subsequently sustained intense erosion. Several watercourses radiate from The Cheviot.
